title: The Two Machines in One Model
lede: The interactive 3D model holds both Kronos designs, the Hyperion breeder and the tandem-mirror burner, as fully explorable geometry.
body: The Kronos 3D model is a single interactive scene that carries two distinct machines. The first is Hyperion, a deuterium-tritium spherical tokamak that breeds tritium. The second is the burner, a deuterium-helium-3 tandem-mirror generator that runs in two housings, Aegis for fixed defense sites and MetroVolt for data centers. Both are rendered from the same engineering geometry that underlies the published design, so the shapes you see are the shapes the physics was computed on.

Neither machine has been built. The model is a design and simulation record, not a photograph of hardware. Construction of the first Hyperion unit begins in Q2 2027, and no hardware net-gain claim is made before the first-of-a-kind reaches first tritium around 2030.

Every major component is a selectable object. Clicking a coil, a blanket segment, or the divertor isolates that part, shows its label, and exposes its principal dimensions and material. Cutaway planes let you slice either machine to see the layered structure from first wall outward.

The model is also physics-computable: the geometry ties back to the frozen design parameters, so field-on-axis, coil currents, and layer thicknesses read directly off the parts rather than being decorative captions.
How the two differ at a glance
Hyperion is toroidal, compact, and dominated by a central stack; the burner is a long linear axis with mirror coils at each end.
Hyperion breeds tritium in a lithium-bearing blanket; the burner minimizes neutrons and converts charged-particle energy directly.
Hyperion peaks at 16.84 T on its toroidal-field conductor; the burner reaches 26.49 T in its high-field plugs.
Start with How to Read the 3D Model, then branch into either machine.

title: How to Read the 3D Model
lede: A short guide to selecting components, reading callouts, and moving between the exterior, cutaway, and exploded views.
body: The model uses one consistent grammar across both machines. A single click selects a component and pins its label. A second click on empty space deselects. Selected parts brighten while the rest of the scene dims, so you always know what you are looking at.

Each selection opens a callout panel with four fields: the component name, its role in one line, its principal measurements, and the material class. Measurements are given in SI units, with millimeters for wall and blanket layers and meters for the machine envelope. Magnetic fields are in tesla, currents in mega-amperes.
Exterior: the sealed machine as it would stand assembled.
Cutaway: a section plane removes half the geometry so you can see the layered build from plasma outward.
Exploded: components separate along their assembly axis to show stacking order and interfaces.

Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, and use the reset control to return to the canonical three-quarter view. On the breeder the natural pivot is the machine centerline; on the burner it is the long axis running through both plugs. A scale reference stays visible so parts never lose their true size.

Callouts state design values and their conditions. Where a number is a simulation result rather than a measured one, the panel says so. The model never implies the machine has been operated. It shows what has been designed and computed, and it flags the physics gates that remain before hardware demonstrates net gain.
Signed-in users see additional layers of internal detail; see Public vs Signed-In Detail.

title: Navigating the 3D Model
lede: Orbit, pan, zoom, and framing controls, plus the keyboard and touch shortcuts that make the model quick to explore.
body: The camera orbits a target point rather than the world origin, so whichever component you select becomes the natural center of rotation. This keeps small parts, like a single divertor cassette, from swinging out of frame while you inspect them.
Left drag orbits around the current target.
Right drag or two-finger drag pans the target across the scene.
Scroll or pinch zooms toward the cursor, not the screen center.
Double-click a part to fly the camera to a framed view of it.

Preset views snap the camera to standard engineering angles: a three-quarter hero view, a true elevation, a plan view down the vertical axis, and an on-axis view along the machine centerline. For the burner the on-axis preset looks straight down the mirror axis through both plug throats, which is the fastest way to read the concentric coil structure.

A near clipping control lets you push the view plane into the machine without switching to a full cutaway, useful for peeking behind the toroidal-field coils on Hyperion or between mirror coils on the burner. The far plane is fixed to the full machine envelope so you never lose global context.

The model offers a lightweight geometry mode for slower devices, which decimates fine mesh detail while preserving every selectable component and every measurement. The physics callouts are identical in both modes, because they read from the design record rather than from the mesh.
For the meaning of what you are framing, see How to Read the 3D Model.

title: Cutaway and Section Views
lede: Section planes remove half the machine so the layered build from plasma to cryostat is visible in a single glance.
body: A fusion machine is defined by what it wraps around the plasma. The value of the design lives in the ordering and thickness of its shells: first wall, blanket, shield, vessel, and structure. A cutaway view is the only honest way to show that ordering, because from the outside every fusion device looks like a metal drum.

You can place the section plane on any of the three principal axes and drag it through the machine. On Hyperion the poloidal section, a vertical cut through the machine centerline, is the most informative: it reveals the D-shaped plasma, its negative triangularity, and the concentric layers outboard of it. On the burner the axial section shows how the central cell, plug throats, expander, and converter chain together.
Innermost is the plasma boundary, drawn with its -0.30 triangularity so the D leans the correct way.
Then the first wall, then the tritium-breeding blanket carrying the 1.8 tritium breeding ratio target.
Then the neutron shield, the vacuum vessel, and finally the toroidal-field coil legs and cryostat.

When the section plane is active, each exposed layer shows its own thickness callout at the cut face. This turns the section into a measured drawing rather than an illustration. The numbers are the frozen design values used in the neutronics and structural models.
Sections pair naturally with the exploded view, which shows the same layers separated along their assembly axis.

title: Exploded View and Assembly Order
lede: The exploded view separates components along their assembly axis, showing stacking order, interfaces, and maintenance access.
body: An exploded view spreads a machine's components apart along the directions they are actually assembled. It answers questions a sealed model cannot: what goes in first, what must come out to reach a given part, and where two components share an interface.

Hyperion explodes along two axes. The blanket and shield modules pull radially outward from the plasma, showing the shell ordering. The vertical components, central solenoid and center stack, lift along the machine axis. This makes the maintenance logic legible: outboard blanket segments are designed to be removed radially through vessel ports without disturbing the center stack.

The burner explodes along its single long axis. The central cell separates from the two plug assemblies, the expander pulls away from its plug, and the direct-energy converter and end tank slide off the axis end. This linear order is the whole point of the mirror architecture: components are strung along an axis rather than nested in shells.
Coil-to-structure interfaces show where magnetic loads are carried into the support frame.
Blanket-to-vessel interfaces show coolant and tritium-line penetrations.
Vacuum interfaces show where seals must hold against the plasma chamber pressure.

Because the explosion follows the true assembly axis, the view doubles as an assembly-sequence record. It is one of the ways the model functions as a design record rather than a rendering. Nothing here is built yet; construction begins Q2 2027.
For the sealed layered structure, compare the cutaway view.

title: The Physics-Computable Model
lede: Geometry in the model is tied to the frozen design parameters, so fields, currents, and dimensions read off the parts themselves.
body: Most 3D product models are decorative: a stylist shapes them and captions are pasted on later. The Kronos model is built the other way around. Its geometry is derived from the same parameter set used in the plasma, magnet, and neutronics models, so the dimensions you measure in the scene are the dimensions the physics was solved on.
What is bound to the geometry
Coil bore and conductor cross-section set the field, so the model can report 16.84 T peak on the Hyperion toroidal-field conductor and 8 T on axis.
Plasma current of 9.86 MA is tied to the plasma cross-section and shape.
Blanket layer thicknesses feed the tritium breeding ratio target of 1.8.
The burner plug and throat geometry carry 26.49 T and 17 T respectively.

Because callouts read from the frozen canon rather than from typed-in text, a geometry change and a number change cannot drift apart. If the blanket thickness in the mesh differs from the design record, the model flags a mismatch rather than showing a comfortable but wrong caption.

The model is not a live solver. It does not run a fresh transport calculation when you rotate the camera. It exposes the results of the frozen design studies and lets you inspect the geometry those studies assumed. This is deliberate: it keeps the public model honest about the difference between a design point and a live experiment.
Every performance figure, including the Hyperion Q of 3.424 at 88.7 MW fusion power, is a simulation result for a machine that is not built. The model states this. See The Model as Design Record.

title: Coordinate Systems in the Model
lede: How the toroidal frame of the breeder and the axial frame of the burner are set up so measurements are unambiguous.
body: The two machines have different symmetries, so the model uses two coordinate conventions. Getting these right matters because every measurement callout is expressed in one of them.

Hyperion is nearly axisymmetric about its vertical centerline, so it uses a cylindrical frame with three coordinates: major radius R measured outward from the centerline, height Z measured up and down from the midplane, and toroidal angle phi around the machine. Plasma shape parameters, triangularity and elongation, live in the R-Z plane, which is why the poloidal cutaway is the canonical shape view.

The burner is a long linear device, so it uses an axial frame: distance s along the mirror axis, radius r from that axis, and azimuth theta around it. Components are located by their s-position, so the callout for a plug throat reports where along the axis it sits and how tightly the field lines pinch there.
Hyperion's origin sits on the centerline at the plasma midplane, so Z is symmetric about zero.
The burner's origin sits at the center of the central cell, so the two plugs are symmetric in positive and negative s.

Publishing the frame is part of keeping the model a usable engineering record. A reader who wants to check a coil position against the design paper needs to know exactly what R, Z, or s a callout refers to. See Units and Scale for how those coordinates are dimensioned.

title: Units and Scale in the Model
lede: The model uses SI units throughout, with a persistent scale reference so components never lose their true size.
body: Every measurement in the model is SI. Machine envelopes and coil positions are in meters, wall and blanket layers in millimeters, magnetic fields in tesla, currents in mega-amperes, and temperatures in kelvin where cryogenics are involved. There is no imperial fallback, which keeps callouts directly comparable to the design papers.

A scale bar and a human-height reference stay in the scene at all zoom levels. This matters more than it sounds: a spherical tokamak and a tandem mirror look superficially similar in a cropped render, but they differ greatly in proportion. The reference keeps the compact, low-aspect-ratio character of Hyperion and the long linear character of the burner honest.
First wall and blanket thicknesses are shown in millimeters at the cut face.
Coil bore and machine radii are shown in meters.
Fields such as 16.84 T peak and 8 T on axis appear in tesla against the conductor and the plasma centerline respectively.

Callouts show the precision the design record carries. A field quoted as 26.49 T for the burner plug is shown to that precision because the design study resolves it; an envelope dimension may be shown to the nearest tenth of a meter because that is the meaningful figure at the machine scale. The model does not invent significant digits.

Because the geometry is the design geometry, apparent size in the scene is true relative size. See Coordinate Systems for how positions are measured, and The Physics-Computable Model for where the numbers come from.

title: Public vs Signed-In Detail
lede: The model shows a full public teaser with real geometry and physics, and reveals deeper internal detail to signed-in users.
body: The 3D model ships in two tiers. The public tier is genuinely useful: it carries the true machine geometry, every major selectable component, the frozen physics callouts, and the cutaway and exploded views. Nothing in the public tier is faked or dumbed down. The signed-in tier adds a further layer of internal engineering detail.
Complete exterior and layered cutaway geometry for both machines.
Selectable major components with role, principal dimensions, and material class.
Frozen canon physics: field on axis, plasma current, breeding ratio target, plug field.
Assembly order via the exploded view.
Finer subassembly breakdown, for example individual blanket sub-modules and coil turn structure.
Additional internal dimensions and interface detail used in the engineering models.

The split protects genuinely detailed engineering work while keeping the public model honest and complete enough to be trusted. It is not a paywall on the science: the physics basis is public. It is a boundary around fine buildable detail, consistent with the design being an active program whose first construction begins Q2 2027.
Neither tier carries any cost, price, or financial figure. The model is an engineering and physics record only. For how the two tiers stay consistent, see The Model as Design Record.

title: The Model as Design Record
lede: The 3D model is a versioned design and simulation record of two unbuilt machines, not a depiction of existing hardware.
body: The most important thing to understand about the Kronos 3D model is what it is a record of. It is the current design state of two machines that do not yet physically exist. Hyperion and the burner are design and simulation work. Construction of the first Hyperion unit begins in Q2 2027, and no hardware net-gain claim is made before the first-of-a-kind reaches first tritium around 2030.
Why a model can be a record

Because the geometry is bound to the frozen design parameters, the model captures a self-consistent snapshot: these shapes, these fields, these layer thicknesses, computed together. That snapshot is a citable artifact in the same sense a drawing set is. It can be versioned, compared against a prior state, and checked against the published physics.
The geometry matches the design the physics was solved on.
Performance figures such as Q 3.424 and 88.7 MW are simulation results, labeled as such.
Physics gates that remain open before net gain are stated, not hidden.

The model never implies operation. There is no rendered plasma glow standing in for a demonstrated shot, no dial reading out a measurement that has not been made. Where a value is a target rather than a result, the callout says target. This restraint is what lets the model be trusted as a record.

Treating the model as a record, and saying plainly that the machines are unbuilt, is a deliberate stance. See The Physics-Computable Model for how the numbers stay bound to the geometry, and Versioning and Provenance for how snapshots are tracked.

title: The Component Labeling System
lede: A consistent naming and tagging scheme lets every part in both machines be selected, cited, and cross-referenced.
body: A model with hundreds of selectable parts needs disciplined naming or it becomes unusable. Every component in the Kronos model carries a stable name and a machine tag, so a reader can say exactly which part they mean: the Hyperion toroidal-field coil, not just the coil.
A machine tag: Hyperion for the breeder, or the burner, with the housing noted where relevant (Aegis or MetroVolt).
A system name: magnet, blanket, vessel, divertor, heating, and so on.
A component name within that system, unique inside its machine.

Components are named by function, following the Kronos convention of describing the breeder as Hyperion and the burner by its housings rather than folding the function into a parenthetical. A part is the breeding blanket because it breeds tritium, not merely because it sits at a radius. This keeps the label meaningful even out of context.

Because names are stable, the library can link directly to a component. A page about the neutron shield can point at the vessel it protects, and the model can highlight both when the link is followed. The labeling system is what makes the model and this library one connected reference rather than two separate resources.

A stable name plus a model version is enough to cite a component unambiguously in a design discussion. This is another way the model functions as a design record. For how versions are tracked, see Versioning and Provenance.

title: Level of Detail in the Model
lede: The model swaps mesh detail by distance and device speed while keeping every selectable part and every measurement intact.
body: A machine this complex cannot render every fastener at once on every device. The model uses level-of-detail, or LOD, to show fine geometry where you are looking and simplified geometry elsewhere. This is a rendering technique, and it never changes the engineering content.

When a component is far from the camera, the model draws a coarser mesh. As you fly in, finer detail loads: coil turn structure, blanket sub-module edges, port flanges. Because selection and callouts are attached to the component, not to a particular mesh resolution, you can still click a distant part and read its numbers.
A full mode for capable machines shows the finest available geometry.
A lightweight mode decimates mesh detail for slower devices and touch screens.
Both modes carry identical selectable components and identical physics callouts.

LOD only ever removes visual triangles. It never removes a measurement, changes a dimension, or hides a physics gate. The frozen values, 16.84 T peak, 9.86 MA, tritium breeding ratio 1.8, 26.49 T in the burner plug, are properties of the design record and are unaffected by how many polygons the scene is drawing.

Separating visual detail from engineering content means the model can be fast without becoming misleading. A phone user sees the same true dimensions as a workstation user. See Navigating the Model for switching modes, and The Physics-Computable Model for where callouts live.

title: Measurement Tools in the Model
lede: Point-to-point, radial, and layer-thickness measurement tools let you read true dimensions directly off the geometry.
body: Because the geometry is the design geometry, measurements taken in the model are real design dimensions, not artistic approximations. The model provides three measurement tools that cover the questions engineers actually ask of a machine like this.

The basic tool drops two points and reports the straight-line distance in SI units. Snapping to component surfaces and edges makes it reliable: you can measure the bore of a coil or the span of a vessel port and get the design value, not a hand-eyed guess.
On Hyperion, a radial tool measures outward from the machine centerline, the natural way to check where a blanket layer or coil leg sits in major radius.
On the burner, an axial tool measures along the mirror axis, the natural way to place a plug throat or the converter.

In cutaway view, a layer tool reads the thickness of each shell at the cut face: first wall, blanket, shield, vessel. These are the numbers that drive the neutronics, so being able to measure them directly closes the loop between the picture and the physics behind the tritium breeding ratio of 1.8.

Every measurement resolves against the frozen design record, so two users measuring the same feature get the same number. This is the practical payoff of a physics-computable model: the ruler and the design agree by construction. For how positions are framed, see Coordinate Systems.

title: Hyperion Breeder: Model Overview
lede: The Hyperion model is a compact deuterium-tritium spherical tokamak whose layered shells breed tritium around the plasma.
body: Hyperion is the Kronos breeder: a deuterium-tritium spherical tokamak whose job is to produce more tritium than it consumes while demonstrating fusion gain. In the model it appears as a compact, low-aspect-ratio machine dominated by a slender central stack, with a thick blanket wrapping the plasma to capture neutrons for breeding.
Fusion gain Q of 3.424 at 88.7 MW fusion power (simulation result).
Toroidal field 8 T on axis, 16.84 T peak on the conductor.

A spherical tokamak squeezes the plasma toward the machine axis, giving a low aspect ratio. This raises the plasma pressure that a given magnetic field can hold, which is efficient, but it forces everything through a very tight central column. Much of what makes Hyperion distinctive, the center stack design and the REBCO magnets, follows from managing that tight center.

Start with a poloidal cutaway to see the D-shaped plasma and the shells outboard of it, then select the center stack, the toroidal-field coils, and the blanket in turn. Each opens its own detailed page in this library.
Hyperion is not built. Construction of the first unit begins Q2 2027, with first tritium targeted around 2030. The model is a design record. Continue to the center stack or the breeding blanket.

title: Hyperion Center Stack
lede: The center stack is the slender central column that carries the toroidal-field return, the solenoid, and the inboard shielding.
body: In a spherical tokamak the center stack is the single most demanding structure. It is the narrow column running up the machine axis that packs together the inboard toroidal-field conductor, the central solenoid, inboard shielding, and their cooling, all in the smallest radius the physics will allow. The tighter this column, the more spherical the plasma and the better the confinement, so every millimeter is contested.
The inboard legs of the toroidal-field system, which set the 8 T on-axis field.
The central solenoid used to induce and drive plasma current.
Inboard neutron shielding protecting the conductors.
Coolant paths that remove nuclear and resistive heating.

Hyperion uses high-temperature REBCO superconductor in the center stack. REBCO carries very high current density at high field, which lets the central column be both slender and capable of the 16.84 T peak field the design requires. This is the enabling technology for a compact spherical tokamak; a conventional conductor could not fit the same performance into the same radius.

Selecting the center stack isolates the column and, for signed-in users, breaks it into its concentric layers. The exploded view lifts the stack along the machine axis, which shows how it is intended to be assembled and, eventually, maintained as a unit.

The center stack sees the highest field, high neutron flux, and large structural loads at once. Its design is a central subject of the Hyperion engineering work. Continue to the toroidal-field coils and the central solenoid it houses.

title: Hyperion Toroidal-Field Coils
lede: The toroidal-field coils produce the field that circles the torus, confining the plasma at 8 T on axis and 16.84 T peak.
body: The toroidal-field coils, or TF coils, are the D-shaped magnets that wrap around the plasma the short way to produce a field that runs the long way around the torus. This toroidal field is the backbone of tokamak confinement: it stops charged particles from drifting straight out and, combined with the plasma current, gives the twisted field lines that hold the plasma.
8 T on the plasma axis, the field the confinement is designed around.
16.84 T peak on the conductor itself, on the inboard leg where the coils crowd toward the machine axis.

Because Hyperion is spherical, the inboard legs of the TF coils must pass through the very tight center stack. That is where the field peaks and where the conductor is most stressed, both magnetically and mechanically. The gap between the 8 T on-axis figure and the 16.84 T peak is exactly the price of the compact geometry: field falls off with radius, so the conductor near the axis sees far more than the plasma does.

The TF coils are selectable as a set and, for signed-in users, individually. A field callout attaches the on-axis and peak values to the geometry, so you can see where on the D-shape the peak occurs. The cutaway shows the inboard legs bundled in the center stack and the outboard legs sweeping around the vessel.

TF coils try to spring toward each other and toward the machine axis under their own field, so they need heavy support structure. See the magnet support structure, and the REBCO magnet model for the conductor.

title: Hyperion Poloidal-Field Coils
lede: The poloidal-field coils shape and position the plasma, setting its elongation, its negative triangularity, and its vertical stability.
body: The poloidal-field coils, or PF coils, are the rings that circle the machine horizontally at various heights. Their field runs in the poloidal plane, and their job is to control the plasma's position and cross-sectional shape. Where the TF coils confine, the PF coils sculpt.
Vertical and radial position of the plasma column.
Elongation, how tall the D-shaped cross-section is.
Triangularity, the -0.30 negative value that leans the D inward on Hyperion.
Vertical stability feedback, since an elongated plasma tends to drift up or down.

Hyperion's plasma runs negative triangularity, meaning the D-shape points its flat side outward rather than inward. This shaping can improve edge stability and heat handling, and it is a deliberate design choice carried through the model: the poloidal cutaway draws the plasma with its -0.30 triangularity so the shape is honest. The PF coil currents are what hold that shape.

The PF coil set is selectable ring by ring. Each ring shows its position in the R-Z plane, and the plasma boundary it helps produce is drawn alongside. This is the clearest place to see how coil currents translate into plasma shape, because moving between the coils and the boundary is a single glance in the poloidal view.
The innermost stacked coils form the central solenoid, treated separately because its job is inducing plasma current, not shaping. See the central solenoid and plasma shape.

title: Hyperion Central Solenoid
lede: The central solenoid sits on the machine axis and drives plasma current inductively, acting as the primary of a transformer.
body: The central solenoid is a tall stack of coils running up the machine axis inside the center stack. It works as the primary winding of a transformer: changing its current induces a loop voltage around the torus, and that voltage drives the plasma current. The plasma itself is the single-turn secondary.
Plasma current, 9.86 MA on Hyperion, produces the poloidal field that, with the toroidal field, twists the field lines needed for confinement.
It also heats the plasma ohmically in the early phase.
Its magnitude and profile are central to stability and confinement quality.

A solenoid can only drive current inductively while its own current is still ramping; once it saturates, the inductive drive ends. In a compact spherical tokamak the solenoid is squeezed for space in the center stack, so it holds limited flux. This is why the design pairs the solenoid with non-inductive current drive to sustain the plasma beyond the inductive phase.

The central solenoid is selectable within the center stack. The exploded view lifts it clear along the axis, showing the coil stack and its position relative to the inboard TF legs and inboard shielding it shares the tight central volume with.

Because the solenoid alone cannot sustain a long pulse, Hyperion relies on external current drive to hold the plasma current after startup. See also the poloidal-field coils that share the poloidal system.

title: Hyperion First Wall
lede: The first wall is the plasma-facing surface that takes the heat and particle flux and shields the breeding blanket behind it.
body: The first wall is exactly what its name says: the first solid surface the plasma sees. It lines the inside of the vacuum chamber and stands between the burning plasma and the breeding blanket. Everything the plasma throws off, heat, neutrons, and stray particles, hits the first wall first.
Intense surface heat flux from radiation and escaping particles.
A 14.1 MeV neutron flux from deuterium-tritium fusion passing through it into the blanket.
Sputtering and erosion from plasma-surface interaction.
Thermal cycling as the machine pulses.

The first wall is deliberately thin so it does not absorb the neutrons the blanket needs for breeding, yet it must be robust enough to handle the surface load. This is a real tension in the design: too thick and it steals neutrons from the tritium breeding ratio of 1.8, too thin and it cannot survive. In the model the first wall is drawn as the innermost shell in the cutaway, just millimeters ahead of the blanket.

The first wall is selectable as a shell; its thickness callout appears at the cut face when the section plane is active. Because it is defined in millimeters against a machine measured in meters, the scale reference is important here to appreciate how thin it really is.
Relation to the blanket and divertor
The first wall handles the general chamber surface; the concentrated exhaust load is taken by the divertor. See the breeding blanket immediately behind it and the divertor that handles the exhaust.

title: Hyperion Breeding Blanket
lede: The breeding blanket wraps the plasma to capture fusion neutrons, breed tritium in lithium, and carry away the fusion heat.
body: The breeding blanket is the reason Hyperion is called a breeder. It is the thick lithium-bearing shell surrounding the plasma, and it does three jobs at once: it captures the 14.1 MeV neutrons from deuterium-tritium fusion, it uses those neutrons to breed new tritium from lithium, and it turns the neutron energy into heat.

A fusion neutron striking lithium-6 produces tritium plus helium; striking lithium-7 it can also produce tritium plus a spare neutron. Deuterium-tritium fusion consumes one tritium per reaction, so to keep running the blanket must breed more than one new tritium per fusion. The Hyperion design targets a tritium breeding ratio of 1.8, meaning 1.8 tritons bred per triton burned.
Some bred tritium is lost to decay and processing before it can be reused.
Neutrons are absorbed by structure and coolant instead of lithium.
A ratio above one is needed just to break even; a comfortable margin covers the losses and can start up other units.

The blanket is the dominant shell in the poloidal cutaway. It is selectable as a whole and, for signed-in users, as modules. Its thickness callout drives the neutronics, so the model ties the visible geometry directly to the breeding-ratio result. Blanket modules are designed to be removed radially through vessel ports for maintenance, which the exploded view shows.
The blanket's heat is carried to the balance of plant, and its bred tritium is sent to the tritium plant. See the tritium plant interface and the neutron shield behind the blanket.

title: Hyperion Neutron Shield
lede: The neutron shield sits behind the blanket to protect the vacuum vessel, the superconducting coils, and the structure from radiation.
body: Even a thick breeding blanket does not stop every neutron. The neutron shield is the layer outboard of the blanket whose job is to absorb the remaining flux before it reaches the components that cannot tolerate it, above all the superconducting magnets.
Superconductors lose performance and are damaged by neutron irradiation over time.
The magnets are cold; neutron heating adds to the cryogenic load that must be removed.
Insulation and structure degrade under accumulated dose.
The inboard side is hardest to shield because the center stack is so tight.

On a spherical tokamak the inboard shield competes for the same scarce radius as the TF conductor and the solenoid. There is only so much room in the center stack, so inboard shielding is one of the tightest trade-offs in the machine: enough to protect the conductor for its intended life, thin enough to keep the geometry compact. This trade-off is a recurring subject of the Hyperion engineering work.

The shield appears in the cutaway as the layer between the blanket and the vacuum vessel, with its own thickness callout. Selecting it highlights how it wraps both the outboard blanket and, more thinly, the inboard center stack.
The shield's purpose is defined by what sits behind it: the vacuum vessel and the toroidal-field coils. See the breeding blanket ahead of it.

title: Hyperion Vacuum Vessel
lede: The vacuum vessel is the sealed chamber that holds the plasma in high vacuum and forms the primary confinement boundary.
body: The vacuum vessel is the sealed metal chamber that encloses the plasma. Fusion plasmas exist only in high vacuum, because any stray gas would cool and contaminate them, so the vessel's first duty is to hold that vacuum against atmospheric pressure pushing in. It is also the primary safety boundary containing the plasma and its tritium inventory.
Maintains high vacuum around the plasma.
Provides a structural boundary that resists atmospheric load and electromagnetic forces.
Carries the ports through which heating, fueling, diagnostics, and maintenance reach the plasma.
Forms a confinement barrier for tritium and activated material.

When a plasma disrupts, its current can dump suddenly, inducing large currents in the vessel that interact with the toroidal field to produce strong forces. The vessel must be stiff enough to take these disruption loads without distortion. In the model the vessel is shown as the shell outboard of the neutron shield and inboard of the coils and cryostat.

The vessel is selectable as a shell and, in the exploded view, separates to reveal its port pattern. Because it is the boundary everything passes through, it is the reference frame for locating ports and internal components.
The vessel's penetrations are where the machine connects to the outside world. See vessel ports and the cryostat that encloses the cold structure outside the vessel.

title: Hyperion Divertor
lede: The divertor is the exhaust component that channels heat and helium ash out of the plasma while protecting the chamber walls.
body: Fusion produces helium ash and a large exhaust heat load, and both must leave the plasma without wrecking the walls. The divertor is the component that handles this. It sits at the bottom of the chamber where shaped magnetic field lines guide the plasma edge onto rugged target plates, well away from the main confining region.
The poloidal-field coils create a magnetic separatrix, a boundary beyond which field lines are diverted to the target plates.
Escaping particles and heat flow along those lines to the divertor rather than striking the first wall everywhere.
Helium ash is pumped away at the divertor, keeping the fuel clean.
The concentrated heat load is spread and cooled on purpose-built targets.

The divertor takes one of the highest steady heat fluxes anywhere in the machine, concentrated on narrow strike lines. Managing that flux, by spreading it, radiating some of it before it lands, and cooling the targets aggressively, is one of the hardest engineering problems in any tokamak, and Hyperion is no exception.

The divertor is selectable at the bottom of the poloidal cutaway, where the diverted field lines can be shown meeting the target plates. Its cassette structure is designed for remote removal, which the exploded view lifts out through a lower port.
The divertor geometry is set by the same coils that shape the plasma. See the poloidal-field coils and the first wall that handles the rest of the chamber surface.

title: Hyperion Heating Systems
lede: External heating raises the plasma to fusion temperatures and, with current drive, sustains it beyond the inductive phase.
body: Ohmic heating from the plasma current alone cannot reach fusion temperatures; the plasma becomes a better conductor as it heats, so resistive heating fades. Hyperion therefore relies on external heating systems to drive the plasma to the tens of millions of kelvin where deuterium-tritium fusion runs, and to help sustain it.
Neutral-beam injection fires fast neutral atoms that penetrate the magnetic field, ionize, and deposit their energy in the core.
Radio-frequency heating couples electromagnetic waves tuned to particle resonances into the plasma.
Both methods also drive plasma current non-inductively, extending the pulse past the solenoid's flux limit.

The fusion gain Q of 3.424 is the ratio of fusion power produced, 88.7 MW, to the external heating power put in. Heating power is therefore not just a means to an end but part of the gain figure itself: the less input needed to sustain a given fusion output, the higher Q. This coupling is why heating efficiency matters as much as heating capacity.

Heating systems are shown as the beam lines and RF launchers entering through the vessel ports. Selecting a heating port highlights its line of sight into the plasma and its penetration through the shield and blanket, which is a real design constraint: every port is a gap in the breeding coverage.
The same systems that heat also sustain current. See current drive and the vessel ports the beams pass through.

title: Hyperion Plasma Shape and Negative Triangularity
lede: Hyperion runs a D-shaped plasma with negative triangularity of -0.30, a shaping choice drawn honestly in the model.
body: A tokamak plasma is not round in cross-section. It is shaped by the poloidal-field coils into a D, described by two main numbers: elongation, how tall it is relative to its width, and triangularity, how much the D-shape leans. Hyperion runs negative triangularity of -0.30.
Positive triangularity points the sharp corner of the D inward, toward the machine axis, the conventional choice.
Negative triangularity, Hyperion's choice, leans the shape the other way, presenting a flatter face outward.
The sign is defined in the R-Z poloidal plane, which is why the poloidal cutaway is the shape view.

Negative triangularity can suppress the edge instabilities that otherwise dump heat onto the wall in bursts, and it can spread the exhaust load more favorably. It is an actively studied route to a better-behaved plasma edge. Choosing it is a considered design decision, and the model commits to it rather than drawing a generic D.

This is one place where model honesty is easy to check: the plasma boundary in the poloidal cutaway is drawn with genuine -0.30 triangularity, leaning the correct way, not a decorative oval. A shape callout reports the triangularity and elongation against the drawn boundary.
The shape is produced entirely by coil currents. See the poloidal-field coils that set it and the divertor whose geometry follows from the same field.

title: Hyperion Cryostat
lede: The cryostat is the outer vacuum enclosure that keeps the superconducting magnets cold by isolating them from ambient heat.
body: Hyperion's magnets are superconducting and must run at cryogenic temperature. The cryostat is the large outer vacuum vessel that surrounds the entire cold structure, magnets and their supports, and holds a vacuum around them. That vacuum is the insulation: with no gas to conduct heat, ambient warmth cannot easily reach the cold mass.
Why it is separate from the vacuum vessel
The vacuum vessel holds vacuum around the plasma, on the inside of the magnets.
The cryostat holds vacuum around the magnets, on the outside.
Two nested vacuum spaces serve two different purposes: plasma confinement and thermal insulation.

Inside the cryostat, thermal shields intercept radiant heat before it reaches the coldest components, and the magnet supports are designed to conduct as little heat as possible from the warm outside world to the cold magnets. Every path for heat to enter is a load the cryogenic plant must remove, so the cryostat and its internals are engineered to minimize those paths.

The cryostat is the outermost large shell in the model, enclosing everything except the external ports and services. Selecting it and switching to cutaway reveals the cold structure inside; hiding it exposes the magnets and vessel for inspection.
The cryostat defines the boundary the cryogenic system works across. See the cryogenic cooling model and the vacuum vessel it encloses.

title: Hyperion Current Drive
lede: Non-inductive current drive sustains the 9.86 MA plasma current after the central solenoid's inductive flux runs out.
body: The central solenoid can only drive plasma current while its own current is ramping, so its inductive drive is finite. To run beyond that, Hyperion must sustain its 9.86 MA plasma current non-inductively, using external systems that push current without relying on a changing solenoid flux.
How current is driven without induction
Neutral-beam injection carries momentum into the plasma in a preferred toroidal direction, dragging current with it.
Radio-frequency waves can be launched to push electrons preferentially one way around the torus.
The plasma also self-generates a bootstrap current from its own pressure gradient, which reduces how much external drive is needed.

A well-shaped, high-pressure plasma spontaneously drives a fraction of its own current, the bootstrap current, arising from the pressure gradient across the confining field. Maximizing this fraction is a design goal because current that the plasma provides for free is current the external systems do not have to supply, which improves the overall gain picture.

Current drive is not a single visible box but a function shared with the heating systems and the plasma itself. The model attributes it to the beam lines and RF launchers at their ports and notes the bootstrap fraction as a plasma property rather than a hardware component.
Why it matters for pulse length
Effective non-inductive drive is what separates a short inductive pulse from a long, steady operation. See the central solenoid whose flux it replaces and the heating systems it shares hardware with.

title: Hyperion Fueling and Pellet Injection
lede: Fueling systems replace burned deuterium and tritium, with frozen pellets fired deep into the plasma to reach the core.
body: A burning plasma consumes deuterium and tritium and must be continuously refueled to keep going. Simply puffing gas at the edge does not work well, because the hot plasma stops cold gas at its boundary before it can reach the core where fusion happens. Hyperion therefore uses pellet injection.
Deuterium and tritium are frozen into small solid pellets.
The pellets are fired at high speed through a vessel port toward the plasma.
A solid pellet penetrates far deeper than gas before it ablates, delivering fuel closer to the core.
The ablated fuel is then ionized and confined.

Fusion power scales steeply with core density, so getting fuel into the core rather than the edge directly affects performance. Pellet fueling also gives control over the density profile, which interacts with confinement and stability. It is a control knob, not just a resupply line.

Fueling is where the breeding loop closes on the machine side. Tritium bred in the blanket, processed by the tritium plant, is frozen into pellets and fired back into the plasma. The tritium breeding ratio of 1.8 exists precisely so this loop can run with margin to spare.
The fueling line is shown entering through a vessel port with its trajectory toward the plasma core. See the vessel ports it uses and the tritium plant interface that supplies its tritium.

title: Hyperion Vessel Ports
lede: Ports are the vessel penetrations that admit heating, fueling, diagnostics, and maintenance access to the plasma.
body: A vacuum vessel would be useless as a sealed box; every system that must reach the plasma does so through a port. Ports are the engineered penetrations through the vessel, and through the shield and blanket around it, that carry heating beams, fueling lines, diagnostics, pumping, and maintenance tooling.
Heating ports for neutral beams and RF launchers.
Diagnostic ports for the instruments that measure the plasma.
Maintenance ports large enough to remove blanket modules and divertor cassettes.

Every port is a hole in the blanket, and a hole in the blanket is a gap in tritium breeding and in shielding. This is a genuine design tension: the machine needs many penetrations to function, yet each one costs breeding coverage and lets neutrons stream toward the magnets. Port count, size, and placement are optimized against the tritium breeding ratio target of 1.8.

Ports are selectable on the vacuum vessel, and selecting one shows what passes through it and how it penetrates the surrounding shells. The exploded view uses the maintenance ports to show how large components are designed to be extracted radially or vertically.
The maintenance ports define how the machine is serviced. See the vacuum vessel they penetrate and the exploded view for the extraction logic.

title: Hyperion Magnet Support Structure
lede: The support structure carries the enormous magnetic forces on the coils, holding the field geometry rigid under load.
body: The magnetic fields in Hyperion do not just confine the plasma; they push hard on the coils that create them. Toroidal-field coils are squeezed toward the machine axis and toward each other, and the whole magnet system carries loads measured in the meganewtons. The support structure is the frame that holds all of this rigid so the field geometry stays where the physics needs it.
TF coils experience a centering force driving their inboard legs toward the axis.
The coils also try to expand outward under their own tension, like a pressurized ring.
PF and solenoid coils push and pull on each other and on the TF set.
Disruptions add sudden transient loads through the vessel.

The centering force converges on the center stack, where the inboard TF legs are packed tightest. Reacting that force without adding radius is one of the defining structural problems of a spherical tokamak: the structure that holds the magnets competes for the same scarce central space as the conductor, the solenoid, and the shielding.

The support structure is selectable as the frame surrounding and bracing the coils. In cutaway it appears as the heavy structural members between and around the magnets; the exploded view shows how the coils seat into it. For signed-in users, load paths are annotated.
Structure and conductor are designed together. See the toroidal-field coils it braces and the center stack where the loads concentrate.

title: Hyperion Tritium Plant Interface
lede: The tritium plant interface extracts bred tritium from the blanket, processes it, and returns clean fuel to the machine.
body: Hyperion breeds its own tritium, so it needs a system to recover that tritium, clean it, and feed it back as fuel. The tritium plant interface is where the machine connects to that fuel-cycle plant. It is the boundary across which bred tritium leaves the blanket and finished fuel returns to the fueling system.
Bred tritium extracted from the breeding blanket.
Tritium and unburned fuel pumped from the plasma exhaust at the divertor.
Processed, isotopically clean deuterium-tritium fuel returning to pellet injection.
Coolant carrying blanket heat, kept separate from the tritium streams.

The tritium breeding ratio of 1.8 is meaningful only if the plant can actually recover the bred tritium faster than it decays and with acceptable losses. The interface and plant are what turn a breeding ratio on paper into a self-sufficient fuel supply, and eventually into surplus tritium that can start other units. Breeding without extraction would be a number with no payoff.

The interface appears as the service connections at the blanket and divertor ports rather than as a single object; the plant itself sits outside the machine envelope. Selecting the interface highlights the extraction and return paths so the fuel loop is visible end to end.
This page covers the machine-side boundary. See the breeding blanket that produces the tritium and the fueling system that returns it.

title: Burner Tandem-Mirror: Model Overview
lede: The burner is a deuterium-helium-3 tandem-mirror generator, a long linear machine with high-field plugs at each end.
body: The Kronos burner is a deuterium-helium-3 tandem-mirror generator. Where Hyperion is a compact ring, the burner is a long straight axis: a central cell where the plasma burns, a high-field magnetic plug at each end to stop the plasma leaking out, an expander beyond each plug, and a direct-energy converter that turns escaping particle energy into usable power. It runs in two housings, Aegis for fixed defense sites and MetroVolt for data centers.
Fuel: deuterium and helium-3, chosen to minimize neutron production.
Neutron fraction 5.44 percent of the fusion power, far below a deuterium-tritium machine.
Plug field 26.49 T; throat field 17 T.
Direct energy conversion of the charged-particle exhaust.
Why a mirror, not a ring

A magnetic mirror confines plasma along a straight axis between two regions of strong field that reflect particles back toward the center. A tandem mirror adds electrostatic plugging at each end to hold particles far better than a simple mirror could. The linear geometry is what makes direct energy conversion natural: charged particles that do escape stream out along the axis, straight into a converter.

This fuel produces most of its energy as charged particles rather than neutrons, which is why the neutron fraction is only 5.44 percent. Fewer neutrons means less activation and shielding, and charged particles can be converted directly to electricity. The trade-off is that the fuel is harder to burn than deuterium-tritium and helium-3 is scarce.
The burner is design and simulation work; no hardware net-gain claim is made before the breeder proves out. Continue to the central cell and the plug throats.

title: Burner Central Cell
lede: The central cell is the long middle region where the deuterium-helium-3 plasma burns, held between the two end plugs.
body: The central cell is the heart of the tandem mirror: the long, relatively uniform-field region in the middle of the machine where the deuterium-helium-3 plasma is confined and fusion takes place. It is the equivalent of the plasma ring in a tokamak, unrolled into a straight line.
A long axis of moderate, fairly uniform magnetic field.
The bulk of the fusion-producing plasma volume.
Bounded at each end by a high-field plug throat that reflects escaping particles.
The region whose length and density set the fusion power.

A plasma in a simple mirror leaks out the ends too readily. The tandem mirror surrounds the central cell with end plugs that create an electrostatic potential barrier, holding the central-cell ions in far more effectively than magnetic mirroring alone. The central cell is therefore designed around what the plugs can hold: its density and temperature are chosen so the plugging can confine them.

The central cell is the long selectable section spanning most of the machine axis. The axial cutaway shows its uniform-field coils and the plasma column running through them, tapering into the plug throats at each end. Its length is a headline dimension because it scales directly with fusion output.
The central cell only works because of the structures at each end. See the high-field plug throats that confine it and the mirror coils that produce the field.

title: Burner High-Field Plug Throats
lede: The plug throats are the intense high-field regions at each end that reflect plasma back into the central cell.
body: At each end of the central cell the magnetic field is squeezed to a very high value in a short region called the plug throat. A charged particle moving from weak field into strong field is turned around, the magnetic mirror effect, so the throats act as stoppers that reflect central-cell plasma back inward instead of letting it stream out the ends.
The plug reaches 26.49 T, the highest field anywhere in either Kronos machine.
The ratio between the throat field and the central-cell field, the mirror ratio, sets how well particles are reflected.
Why the field must be so high

Confinement in a mirror improves with the mirror ratio, the jump from central-cell field to peak plug field. A higher peak field turns back a larger fraction of particles, so pushing the plug to 26.49 T directly buys confinement. Reaching that field is why the burner, like Hyperion, depends on high-temperature REBCO superconductor; no conventional magnet reaches it in this geometry.

The high field alone is not enough for a fusion-grade device, so the plugs also establish an electrostatic potential that repels central-cell ions. The throat is where the magnetic and electrostatic confinement combine. This is the defining feature of a tandem mirror and the reason the plug region is the most demanding part of the machine.

The plug throats are selectable at each end of the axis, with the 26.49 T and 17 T callouts attached to the geometry. The axial cutaway shows the field lines pinching through the throat. See the mirror coils that produce the field and the expander beyond the throat.

title: Burner Expander
lede: The expander is the flaring region beyond each plug where the escaping plasma spreads out along widening field lines.
body: No mirror is perfect; some plasma always escapes past the plug throats. The expander is the region beyond each throat where the magnetic field deliberately weakens and the field lines flare apart. As the field drops, the escaping plasma spreads across a much larger area, which is exactly what the next stage needs.
Concentrated plasma leaving the throat would deliver a punishing heat load onto a small area.
Spreading it across a wide expander surface reduces the power density to manageable levels.
The expansion also sorts the particle flow in a way that prepares it for direct energy conversion.
It provides room to handle the exhaust without eroding a small target.

Because charged particles follow field lines, widening the field lines widens the plasma stream. The expander is essentially a magnetic nozzle run in reverse: instead of focusing the flow, it dilutes it. The degree of expansion is a design parameter, set by how much the field is allowed to fall from the throat value of 17 T out to the converter.

The expander is the flaring section between each plug throat and its end assembly. In the axial cutaway the field lines can be shown fanning outward through it, and the growing cross-section is visible directly. Selecting it reports the expansion and the resulting drop in power density onto the converter.
The spread-out plasma flows into the converter. See the direct-energy converter it feeds and the plug throats it follows.

title: Burner Direct-Energy Converter
lede: The direct-energy converter turns the kinetic energy of escaping charged particles into electricity without a thermal cycle.
body: Most power plants convert heat to electricity through a steam cycle, which throws away a large fraction of the energy as waste heat. The burner can do better because its deuterium-helium-3 fuel produces charged particles, and charged particles carry electrical charge that can be harvested directly. The direct-energy converter does exactly this.
Charged particles streaming out through the expander enter a region of biased electrodes.
Moving against an electric field, the particles give up their kinetic energy to that field, decelerating.
Collected on the electrodes, they deliver their energy as electrical current at high voltage.
No intermediate heat-to-motion-to-electricity chain is needed.
Why the fuel choice enables it

Direct conversion only works on charged particles; neutrons carry no charge and cannot be converted this way. This is the payoff of the deuterium-helium-3 fuel and its 5.44 percent neutron fraction: with most of the fusion energy in charged particles, most of it is available to a direct converter. A neutron-heavy fuel would leave little for direct conversion to catch.

The converter is selectable at the end of each expander, shown as the array of collector electrodes facing the incoming plasma flow. The axial cutaway lines it up with the throat and expander so the whole escape-and-convert path reads as one chain along the axis.
Whatever is not converted must be pumped and handled. See the end tanks behind the converter and the expander that feeds it.

title: Burner End Tanks
lede: The end tanks terminate each end of the machine, housing the converter, handling exhaust, and maintaining the axial vacuum.
body: The end tanks are the large vacuum chambers that cap each end of the burner's long axis. They enclose the direct-energy converter, provide the volume the expanded plasma flows into, pump away neutral gas and unconverted particles, and hold the vacuum that the whole linear plasma requires.
House the direct-energy converter and its electrodes.
Provide the large volume the expander flow needs.
Pump exhaust gas and helium ash to keep the plasma clean.
Maintain the axial vacuum against gas load.

A linear machine has two open ends where plasma and neutral gas collect, so the end tanks carry a heavy pumping duty. Keeping the pressure low there prevents neutral gas from streaming back up the axis into the central cell and cooling the burn. The tanks are sized for this pumping load as much as for the converter they hold.

The burner is symmetric about the center of its central cell, so there is an end tank at each end, each with its own throat, expander, and converter. In the coordinate frame the two tanks sit at positive and negative extremes of the axial coordinate, mirror images across the origin at the central cell's center.

The end tanks are the large chambers terminating each end of the model. Selecting one and cutting away reveals the converter inside and the pumping connections. See the direct-energy converter they house and the burner overview for the full axis.

title: Burner Mirror Coils
lede: The mirror coils shape the axial field, gentle in the central cell and intense at the plugs, to confine the plasma.
body: A tandem mirror is defined by its magnetic field profile along the axis: moderate in the central cell, then rising steeply to a peak at each plug throat, then falling in the expander. The mirror coils are the ring magnets strung along the axis that produce this profile. Their spacing and current set where the field is weak, where it peaks, and how sharply it changes.
Central-cell coils produce a long region of moderate, fairly uniform field.
Plug coils produce the intense fields, up to 26.49 T at the plug and 17 T at the throat.
Expander coils let the field flare down beyond the throat.
All are wound from high-temperature REBCO superconductor to reach the required fields.

The single most important number the coils set is the mirror ratio: the peak plug field divided by the central-cell field. A larger ratio reflects more particles and confines better, which is why the plug coils are pushed to such extreme fields. The whole coil layout is an exercise in achieving a high mirror ratio without the field changing so abruptly that it drives instabilities.

The mirror coils are selectable individually or as families along the axis. The axial cutaway can plot the field magnitude against position so you can see the moderate central plateau rising to the 26.49 T plug peak. This is the clearest way to read how coil placement becomes confinement.
The coils use the same REBCO conductor as Hyperion's magnets. See the REBCO magnet model and the plug throats the plug coils produce.

title: Burner Plasma Confinement Geometry
lede: Confinement in the burner combines magnetic mirroring with electrostatic plugging along a single straight axis.
body: The burner confines its plasma along a straight axis rather than around a ring, which changes the whole geometry of the problem. Instead of twisting field lines to trap particles on nested surfaces, a mirror machine traps them between two regions of strong field and, in a tandem, behind two electrostatic barriers.
Magnetic mirroring: particles moving into rising field are reflected, held between the two plug throats.
Electrostatic plugging: the plugs establish a potential that repels central-cell ions, plugging the leaks the magnetic mirror alone would allow.
Together these confine the central-cell plasma far better than either mechanism alone.

A simple mirror always leaks particles whose velocity is aligned closely enough with the axis to slip through the throat, the loss cone. The tandem's electrostatic barrier narrows this loss, but confinement in any mirror is ultimately about minimizing loss-cone leakage. The escaping particles are not purely waste, though: they are the stream the direct-energy converter harvests.
Why the linear geometry pays off

The open-ended geometry that makes confinement harder is the same geometry that makes direct energy conversion easy. Particles that escape do so along the axis, straight out through the expander into the converter. The burner turns the mirror's classic weakness, end losses, into the mechanism by which it produces electricity.

The axial cutaway shows the field profile and the confined plasma column, with the loss stream continuing through the expander. See the plug throats that do the confining and the coordinate systems that frame the axis.

title: Burner Neutron Fraction and Shielding
lede: Deuterium-helium-3 fuel keeps neutrons to 5.44 percent of the fusion power, easing shielding compared with deuterium-tritium.
body: The primary deuterium-helium-3 reaction produces a proton and a helium-4 nucleus, both charged, and no neutron. The burner still makes some neutrons from side reactions, chiefly deuterium burning with deuterium, but far fewer than a deuterium-tritium machine. The design carries a neutron fraction of 5.44 percent of the fusion power.
Neutrons activate materials and require heavy shielding; fewer neutrons means less activation.
Charged particles can be converted directly to electricity, neutrons cannot.
Lower neutron flux eases the burden on structure and magnets over the machine's life.
The remaining 5.44 percent still requires real shielding, so it is not zero.

A low neutron fraction is a genuine advantage, but it is not a neutron-free machine, and the model does not pretend otherwise. The 5.44 percent still demands shielding around the central cell and structural attention to activation. Deuterium-helium-3 also burns less readily than deuterium-tritium and helium-3 is scarce, so the low-neutron benefit is paid for elsewhere.

Shielding appears around the central cell where most neutrons originate, thinner than a comparable deuterium-tritium blanket would be because there is less flux to stop. Selecting the shield reports the neutron fraction it is sized against. The contrast with Hyperion's thick breeding blanket is visible directly when the two machines are compared.
See the deuterium-helium-3 fuel cycle for why the neutron fraction is low, and the Hyperion blanket for the deuterium-tritium contrast.

title: Burner Deuterium-Helium-3 Fuel Cycle
lede: The burner fuses deuterium with helium-3, a reaction that releases its energy mostly as charged particles.
body: The burner runs on deuterium and helium-3. When they fuse, they produce a proton and a helium-4 nucleus, releasing about 18.3 MeV of energy carried entirely by charged particles. This is the reaction that makes direct energy conversion and low neutron output possible.
The main reaction produces no neutron, so most energy is in charged particles.
Charged-particle energy can be captured directly by the converter.
Low neutron output means less activation and lighter shielding, the 5.44 percent design fraction.

Deuterium-helium-3 is much harder to burn than deuterium-tritium: it needs higher temperatures and better confinement to reach useful reaction rates, which is part of why the burner uses such extreme plug fields. Deuterium will also fuse with itself, and those side reactions are the source of the residual neutrons. And helium-3 is genuinely scarce, which is a real constraint on the fuel supply rather than an afterthought.

A tandem mirror pairs naturally with this fuel. The high fields needed for confinement also enable the high mirror ratio, and the open linear geometry sends escaping charged particles straight into a direct converter. The fuel and the machine architecture reinforce each other: the charged-particle output is only useful because the geometry can catch it.

The fuel cycle is represented by the fueling and exhaust connections at the central cell and end tanks rather than a single part. See the neutron fraction and shielding and the direct-energy converter that the fuel choice enables.

title: Burner Aegis Housing
lede: Aegis is the burner packaged for fixed defense installations, the same tandem-mirror generator in a site-hardened enclosure.
body: Aegis is the burner configured for fixed defense installations. It is not a different reactor; it is the same deuterium-helium-3 tandem-mirror generator, with the same central cell, plugs, expanders, and converters, packaged and hardened for a fixed defense site. Aegis is a fixed installation, not a naval system.
Site hardening and protection appropriate to a defense installation.
Integration with the power needs of a fixed base.
The layout and services a permanent site requires.
The same core physics as the MetroVolt housing.

The distinction the model draws is between the machine and its housing. The tandem-mirror generator is common; Aegis and MetroVolt differ in the enclosure, siting, and balance-of-plant around that common core. This is why the naming keeps the function, burner, primary and treats Aegis and MetroVolt as housings of it rather than as separate machines.

Selecting the Aegis housing wraps the burner in its site-appropriate enclosure while leaving the internal machine identical to the MetroVolt view. Switching between housings changes the packaging you see, not the plug field of 26.49 T or the 5.44 percent neutron fraction, which belong to the machine.
For the data-center configuration of the same generator, see the MetroVolt housing, and the burner overview for the shared machine.

title: Burner MetroVolt Housing
lede: MetroVolt is the burner packaged for data centers, delivering the tandem-mirror generator as an on-site power source.
body: MetroVolt is the burner configured for data centers. As with Aegis, the reactor itself is unchanged: the same deuterium-helium-3 tandem-mirror generator with the same central cell, high-field plugs, expanders, and direct-energy converters. What differs is the housing, siting, and integration suited to supplying a data center's power demand.
Integration with the continuous, high-density power needs of a data center.
A layout appropriate to a commercial computing site.
The same machine core as the Aegis housing.

Data centers need large, steady, reliable power, and a compact generator that can sit near the load reduces dependence on the surrounding grid. The direct-energy converter's ability to produce electricity without a full thermal cycle is part of what makes the burner attractive for this role. The model presents the generation principle; it carries no economic or performance-per-site claims.

Selecting the MetroVolt housing shows the burner in its data-center enclosure. Toggling to Aegis keeps the internal machine identical and swaps only the packaging, which is the clearest demonstration that the two are one machine in two housings. The physics callouts, 26.49 T plug, 17 T throat, 5.44 percent neutron fraction, are unchanged between them.
The other housing and the machine
See the Aegis housing for the defense configuration and the burner overview for the shared generator.

title: Burner Heating Systems
lede: The burner uses radio-frequency and neutral-beam heating to reach the high temperatures deuterium-helium-3 fusion demands.
body: Deuterium-helium-3 needs higher temperatures than deuterium-tritium to fuse at a useful rate, so the burner's heating systems must work hard. They raise the central-cell plasma to the required conditions and help establish the plasma potential that the tandem plugging depends on.
Radio-frequency heating couples electromagnetic waves at particle resonances into the plasma, including electron-cyclotron heating tuned to the strong-field regions.
Neutral-beam injection fires fast neutral atoms that penetrate and deposit energy in the plasma.
Heating in the plug regions helps build the electrostatic potential that plugs the central cell.

In a tandem mirror, heating is not only about temperature. Selectively heating the plug plasma raises its density and potential, which strengthens the electrostatic barrier that confines the central cell. Heating is therefore part of the confinement scheme, not just a way to reach ignition-relevant temperatures. This coupling is specific to the mirror architecture.

Heating systems appear as the launchers and beam lines entering the central cell and plug regions. Selecting one shows where its power is deposited along the axis, which matters because central-cell heating and plug heating serve different purposes. The high-field regions are natural targets for electron-cyclotron heating because the resonance follows the field strength.
Because heating and plugging are linked, this system connects directly to confinement. See the confinement geometry and the plug throats the heating supports.

title: The Shared REBCO Magnet Model
lede: Both Kronos machines rely on REBCO high-temperature superconductor to reach fields conventional magnets cannot deliver.
body: The single technology that makes both Kronos machines possible is the same: high-temperature superconducting magnets wound from REBCO tape. REBCO stands for rare-earth barium copper oxide, a ceramic superconductor that carries large current at high magnetic field and at temperatures well above those older superconductors need.
It sustains superconductivity at high field, where older conductors quench, reaching Hyperion's 16.84 T peak and the burner's 26.49 T plug.
It carries very high current density, letting magnets be compact, which is essential for a spherical tokamak's tight center stack.
It operates at higher temperature than low-temperature superconductors, easing the cryogenic system.

Hyperion winds REBCO into D-shaped toroidal-field coils and a central solenoid; the burner winds it into ring mirror coils, with the most extreme windings in the plugs. The conductor and its challenges, tape architecture, winding, quench protection, and cooling, are shared, which is why the model treats REBCO as a common subsystem across both machines.

The REBCO magnet model is accessible from both machines. Selecting a coil in either can drill into its conductor structure, and for signed-in users into the turn and tape detail. This shared view is the clearest place to see that the two very different machines rest on one magnet technology.
See the tape architecture, the coil winding model, the quench protection, and the cryogenic cooling that keeps it superconducting.

title: REBCO Tape Architecture
lede: REBCO conductor is a thin layered tape: a superconducting film on a metal substrate, protected by silver and copper.
body: REBCO is not a wire but a tape: a thin, flat, layered ribbon a few millimeters wide. The superconductor itself is a microns-thin ceramic film, and the rest of the tape exists to support that film, carry current when it is not superconducting, and protect it. Understanding this layered structure explains most of what is hard about REBCO magnets.
A strong metal substrate that gives the tape its mechanical strength.
Buffer layers that let the ceramic grow with the right crystal alignment on the metal.
The REBCO superconducting film, only microns thick, which carries the current.
A silver cap and copper stabilizer that protect the film and carry current if it stops superconducting.

The superconducting film must have its crystal grains well aligned, or its current-carrying capacity collapses; the buffer layers exist to achieve that alignment. The copper stabilizer is a safety layer: if a spot warms and stops superconducting, current can flow briefly through the copper instead of causing damage. This interplay is central to both performance and quench protection.

For signed-in users the model can expand a coil down to its tape cross-section, showing the layer stack. This is deep detail reserved for the signed-in tier, but the principle, that the current lives in a microns-thin film on a supporting tape, is explained in the public tier because it is essential to understanding the magnets.
Tapes are stacked and wound into coils. See the coil winding model and the quench protection that the copper stabilizer supports.

title: REBCO Coil Winding Model
lede: Coils are built by stacking and winding REBCO tapes into turns, then into pancakes, insulated and clamped against huge forces.
body: A single REBCO tape carries a useful but limited current. To make a magnet, many tapes are combined and wound into turns, and many turns are stacked into a coil. The winding pattern, how the tapes are laid, insulated, and supported, determines the field the coil produces and whether it survives the forces that field creates.
Tapes are stacked or cabled to carry the required total current.
Turns are wound in a defined pattern, often as flat pancake sections stacked together.
Insulation, or in some designs deliberately reduced insulation, is placed between turns.
The whole coil is clamped in structure to react the magnetic forces.

A design choice in REBCO coils is how much to insulate between turns. Fully insulated coils force all current along the intended path; no-insulation coils let current cross between turns, which can protect the coil during a quench by spreading current away from a hot spot, at the cost of slower response. This trade-off is one of the active engineering questions in high-field REBCO magnets.

The winding structure is signed-in detail. A selected coil can be expanded to show its turn and pancake layout, letting you see how the conductor path builds up the field. In the public tier the coil is shown as a solid magnet with its field callout, sufficient to understand its role without the fine winding detail.
Wound coils must be held against enormous forces and kept cold. See the magnet support structure, the quench protection, and the cryogenic cooling.

title: Magnet Quench Protection Model
lede: A quench is a sudden loss of superconductivity; protection systems detect it early and safely dissipate the stored energy.
body: A quench is when part of a superconducting coil suddenly stops superconducting and becomes resistive. The current keeps flowing, now through resistance, so that spot heats rapidly. In a high-field magnet storing large energy, an undetected quench can concentrate that energy in a small volume and damage the coil. Quench protection is the set of measures that prevent this.
Detect the quench quickly, before the hot spot grows dangerous.
Spread the heating over as much of the coil as possible instead of one point.
Dump the coil's stored magnetic energy safely, often into an external resistor.
Do all of this in the short time before damage occurs.

REBCO quenches are harder to handle than in older superconductors because the normal zone spreads slowly. A resistive spot stays local rather than propagating along the conductor, so it is harder to detect and more prone to concentrating heat. This is why REBCO magnet design pays so much attention to detection speed and to design choices, such as reduced insulation, that let current find its own way around a hot spot.

Quench protection is a system rather than a single visible part, so the model represents it through the coil design features that enable it, the copper stabilizer in the tape and the winding scheme, and through annotations for signed-in users. The public tier explains the principle because it is central to why these magnets are hard to build.
Why it belongs to both machines
Both Hyperion and the burner run high-field REBCO magnets, so both need quench protection. See the tape architecture whose stabilizer helps and the coil winding that sets the response.

title: Cryogenic Cooling Model
lede: The cryogenic system keeps the REBCO magnets cold enough to stay superconducting despite nuclear and ambient heat loads.
body: REBCO only superconducts below a critical temperature that depends on the field it carries. The cryogenic cooling system's job is to hold the magnets safely below that limit at all times, removing every watt of heat that leaks in or is generated within. If the temperature rises too far, the magnet quenches.
Radiant and conducted heat leaking in from the warm surroundings.
Nuclear heating from neutrons that reach the magnets despite shielding.
Heat from joints and current leads carrying power into the cold mass.
Any resistive heating from imperfect superconductivity.

One reason REBCO is attractive is that it superconducts at higher temperatures than older conductors, so it can be cooled with less demanding refrigeration. Higher operating temperature also means more margin: the magnet can absorb a little more heat before reaching its critical temperature. This margin is part of what makes high-field REBCO magnets practical rather than merely possible.

The cryostat provides the insulating vacuum around the cold mass, and the cooling loop, coolant circulated through the coils and thermal shields, carries heat out to the refrigeration plant. The two work together: the cryostat minimizes the heat that gets in, and the cooling loop removes what remains. On Hyperion the neutron shield further reduces the nuclear heat load on the magnets.
Cooling is shown through the cryostat boundary and the cooling connections to the coils. See the cryostat that insulates the cold mass and the quench protection that acts if cooling margin is lost.

title: Component Measurements and Design Parameters
