lede: Every component carries measurements and design parameters drawn from the frozen canon, readable directly in the model.
body: Selecting any component opens its measurements and design parameters: dimensions, materials, and the physics values that define its role. These are not captions typed alongside the geometry; they are drawn from the frozen design record, so the picture and the numbers cannot disagree.
Hyperion: Q 3.424 at 88.7 MW fusion power, 9.86 MA plasma current, 8 T on axis, 16.84 T peak conductor field, negative triangularity -0.30, tritium breeding ratio 1.8.
Burner: 26.49 T plug field, 17 T throat field, 5.44 percent neutron fraction, direct energy conversion.

Below the machine headlines, each component carries its own numbers: layer thicknesses in millimeters for the first wall, blanket, and shield; coil bore and position in meters; field values in tesla at the conductor; axial positions along the burner. In cutaway, layer thicknesses appear at the cut face; on a selected coil, its field callout appears against the conductor.

The model distinguishes simulation results from design targets. The Q of 3.424 is a simulation result for an unbuilt machine; the tritium breeding ratio of 1.8 is a design target the blanket is sized to meet. Callouts label which is which, so no reader mistakes a computed design point for a measured one.

Because every value traces to the frozen canon, the same number appears wherever the component does, in the model, in this library, and in the design papers. See The Physics-Computable Model and Design Parameter Callouts.

title: Design Parameter Callouts
lede: Callouts present a component's key parameters with their conditions, so a number is never shown without the context it needs.
body: A fusion parameter without its conditions can mislead. A field value means little without saying where it is measured; a gain figure means little without saying against what input. The model's callouts always pair a number with the condition that makes it meaningful, following the Kronos practice of quoting frozen values together with their caveats.
Field 8 T on axis, 16.84 T peak on the conductor, two values because the field varies with radius.
Q 3.424 at 88.7 MW fusion power, a simulation result, gain stated against the power it refers to.
26.49 T at the burner plug, 17 T at the throat, each tied to its location on the axis.
Neutron fraction 5.44 percent of fusion power, the denominator stated explicitly.

Stating conditions keeps the model honest and keeps its numbers usable. A reader can carry a callout into the design papers and check it, because they know exactly what it refers to. It also prevents the common failure of quoting a peak conductor field as if it were the field the plasma sees, or a fusion gain as if it were a net-electric gain.

Where a parameter depends on a physics gate that has not been demonstrated, the callout says so. The model makes no hardware net-gain claim before the first Hyperion unit reaches first tritium around 2030, and its callouts reflect that: computed design points are labeled as computed, not as achieved.
Callouts appear on selection and expand in cutaway. See Component Measurements for the full parameter set and The Model as Design Record for the honesty stance behind them.

title: Model Versioning and Provenance
lede: Each model release is a versioned snapshot tied to a frozen design state, so any component can be cited unambiguously.
body: Because the 3D model is a design record, it is versioned like one. Each release is a snapshot of a specific frozen design state: these dimensions, these fields, these layer thicknesses, computed together. A version identifier lets a reader know exactly which design the geometry represents and check it against the design papers of the same state.
The geometry of every component at that design state.
The frozen parameter values the callouts report.
The correspondence between the model and the published design work.
A stable reference for citing a component.

Provenance is the record of where the geometry and numbers came from. Each version traces its parameters back to the frozen canon and, through it, to the physics and engineering models that produced them. This chain is what lets the model be used in a design discussion: a claim about a component can be followed back to its source rather than taken on faith.
Why it matters for two tiers

The public and signed-in tiers of a given version describe the same design state at different levels of detail, so a signed-in dimension and a public dimension of the same part always agree. Versioning is what keeps the two tiers consistent, and what lets an update to the design propagate cleanly to both.
A component name plus a version identifier is a stable citation. See the component labeling system for the naming and The Model as Design Record for why the model is treated this way.

title: Comparing the Breeder and Burner in the Model
lede: Viewing Hyperion and the burner side by side shows how differently two fusion machines can be built for different jobs.
body: Placing Hyperion and the burner side by side in the model is the fastest way to understand that fusion is not one machine but a family of designs. Both confine hot plasma with magnetic fields, yet almost everything else about them differs because they are built for different jobs: one breeds tritium, the other generates power with minimal neutrons.
Hyperion is a compact torus dominated by a central stack; the burner is a long straight axis.
Hyperion confines on nested toroidal surfaces; the burner confines between mirror plugs along a line.
Hyperion wraps a thick breeding blanket; the burner keeps thin shielding and open ends for direct conversion.

Hyperion burns deuterium-tritium, which is easier to ignite but neutron-heavy, so it needs a thick blanket that turns those neutrons into bred tritium at a breeding ratio of 1.8. The burner burns deuterium-helium-3, which is harder to ignite but keeps neutrons to 5.44 percent, so it can convert charged particles directly instead of breeding.

Both push high-temperature REBCO magnets hard, but differently: Hyperion peaks at 16.84 T on its toroidal-field conductor with 8 T on axis, while the burner reaches 26.49 T in its plugs and 17 T at the throats. The shared conductor technology reaching two different extremes is one of the clearest lessons of the side-by-side view.
Load both machines and use the shared scale reference to compare their true proportions. See the breeder overview and the burner overview, and the REBCO magnet model they share.

title: Reading a Poloidal Cutaway
lede: A vertical section through Hyperion's centerline is the single most informative view, showing plasma shape and every shell.
body: If you look at only one view of Hyperion, make it the poloidal cutaway: a vertical section through the machine centerline. Because the machine is nearly axisymmetric, this one slice captures the plasma shape and every shell that wraps it, all in the plane where the physics is naturally described.
The D-shaped plasma boundary with its -0.30 negative triangularity.
The first wall, then the breeding blanket, then the neutron shield, then the vacuum vessel, in order.
The inboard center stack packing the TF legs, solenoid, and inboard shield.
The divertor at the bottom where diverted field lines meet the targets.

Plasma shape parameters, triangularity and elongation, are defined in this R-Z plane, so the poloidal cutaway is where they are honestly visible. The shell ordering is also radial, so a horizontal traverse from the plasma outward crosses each layer once, letting you read the whole build from a single line across the picture.

Start at the plasma and move outward: the thin first wall, the thick blanket carrying the breeding, the shield protecting the magnets, the vessel holding vacuum, then the coils and cryostat. Layer thickness callouts at the cut face turn this into a measured drawing you can compare directly against the neutronics that give the breeding ratio of 1.8.
Each layer has its own page. See the breeding blanket, the plasma shape, and the general cutaway views.

title: Reading an Axial Cutaway
lede: A section along the burner's long axis shows the confine-then-convert chain from central cell to direct converter.
body: For the burner, the equivalent of Hyperion's poloidal cutaway is the axial section: a slice along the machine's long axis. It shows the entire chain of the tandem mirror in order, from the central cell where the plasma burns to the converter where escaping energy becomes electricity.
The central cell, the long region of moderate field where fusion happens.
A high-field plug throat at each end, peaking at 26.49 T in the plug and 17 T at the throat.
The expander beyond each throat, where the field flares and the plasma spreads.
The direct-energy converter and end tank at each end.

The axial cutaway is where the field-versus-position profile makes sense. The section can plot field magnitude along the axis: a moderate plateau through the central cell rising to the sharp plug peak, then falling through the expander. Confinement is written into that curve, because the ratio of the peak to the plateau is the mirror ratio that reflects particles.

The burner is symmetric about the center of the central cell, so the axial cutaway shows a mirror image at each end. Following an escaping particle from the central cell, through the loss cone at the throat, spreading in the expander, and landing on the converter, is the clearest way to see how the machine turns end losses into power.
Each section of the chain has its own page. See the central cell, the plug throats, and the direct-energy converter.

title: Material Annotations in the Model
lede: Each component is tagged with its material class, so the model shows not just where a part is but what it must be made of.
body: What a part is made of

Geometry answers where a component sits; material annotations answer what it must be made of. In a fusion machine the two are inseparable, because the demands on each part, heat, neutron flux, field, cryogenic temperature, dictate the material class as strictly as the shape dictates the fit.
Plasma-facing surfaces on the first wall and divertor, chosen to survive heat and particle bombardment.
Lithium-bearing breeder material in the Hyperion blanket, needed to breed tritium at a ratio of 1.8.
Structural materials that keep strength under neutron irradiation.
REBCO high-temperature superconductor in the magnets of both machines.
Shielding materials sized to absorb the neutron flux each machine produces.
Why the material follows the physics

The blanket must contain lithium because only lithium breeds tritium under neutron bombardment. The magnets must be REBCO because only a high-temperature superconductor reaches 16.84 T or 26.49 T in these geometries. The first wall must resist erosion because it faces the plasma. Each material choice is forced by a physical demand the model can state alongside it.

Selecting a component reports its material class in the callout. Fine material detail and tolerances are reserved for the signed-in tier, but the material class of every major part is public, because knowing what a part is made of is basic to understanding why it is where it is.
See the component measurements that accompany the material tags and the REBCO magnet model for the superconductor material in depth.

title: Isolating and Hiding Components
lede: Isolate a single part or hide obscuring shells to inspect any component of either machine without clutter.
body: A machine of nested shells and stacked coils hides most of itself from any single viewpoint. Two complementary controls solve this: isolating a component to show only it, and hiding components that block the view of something behind them. Together they let you inspect any part without the clutter of everything around it.
Select a component and isolate it to remove everything else from view.
The part keeps its true position and scale, so its context is not lost.
Its callout stays open, so you can read its measurements while it stands alone.
Useful for studying a single coil, a divertor cassette, or one blanket module.

Hiding works the other way: instead of keeping one part, you remove specific parts that are in the way. Hiding the cryostat exposes the magnets; hiding the outboard blanket exposes the first wall and plasma. Hidden parts are tracked so you can restore them, which prevents losing your place in a complex teardown.

Hiding and the section plane complement each other. A cutaway removes half the machine along a plane; hiding removes chosen components regardless of where the plane is. Using both, you can, for example, cut Hyperion in the poloidal plane and then hide the shield to see the blanket and vessel relationship on the cut face directly.
A restore control brings hidden parts back and clears any isolation, returning to the full assembly. See Navigating the Model for the camera controls and Cutaway Views for the section plane.

title: Model Honesty and Physics Gates
lede: The model shows what is designed and computed, states clearly that the machines are unbuilt, and flags the gates that remain.
body: The most important design rule of the Kronos 3D model is honesty about what it is. It represents two machines that have not been built. It shows the design geometry and the computed performance, and it states plainly that these are simulation results, not measurements from operating hardware.
What the model does not do
It does not render a plasma glow as if standing in for a demonstrated shot.
It does not show a dial reading out a measurement that has not been made.
It does not claim hardware net gain before the first Hyperion unit reaches first tritium around 2030.
It does not present a computed design point as an achieved result.

A physics gate is a result that must be demonstrated before a claim can be made. The model flags these rather than glossing over them: the gain figure of Q 3.424 is a simulation result, the tritium breeding ratio of 1.8 is a design target, and the burner's performance rests on confinement that the extreme plug fields are designed to achieve. Naming the gates is what separates a design record from a marketing render.

A model that overstated what exists would undermine the very work it displays. By being explicit that construction begins Q2 2027 and that net gain is not claimed before first tritium, the model can be trusted precisely because it does not exaggerate. Its restraint is what makes its numbers worth citing.
See The Model as Design Record and Design Parameter Callouts for how the numbers are presented with their status.

title: Linking the Model to This Library
lede: Every component in the model connects to an explanatory page here, so geometry and explanation form one reference.
body: The 3D model and this library are designed to work as a single reference. The model shows where a component sits and what it measures; the library explains what it does and why it is built that way. Because the components carry stable names, the two connect directly: a part in the model links to its page here, and a page here can highlight its part in the model.
Selecting a component in the model offers its explanatory page in this library.
A page here can point the model at the component it describes and highlight it.
Both use the same component names, so there is no ambiguity about which part is meant.
Both draw physics values from the same frozen canon, so the numbers match.
Why keep them separate but linked

Geometry and prose are best at different things. A 3D view conveys spatial relationships and scale instantly; written explanation conveys mechanism, purpose, and trade-offs. Rather than cram explanation into cramped model callouts or force a written page to describe a shape in words, each does what it is good at and hands off to the other.

A reader can move fluidly between seeing and understanding: notice the thick blanket in the cutaway, jump to its page to learn why it breeds tritium at a ratio of 1.8, then return to the model to measure its thickness. Neither half is complete alone; together they are a full engineering reference for two unbuilt machines.
Begin at How to Read the 3D Model and the two-machine overview, then follow any component into its page.
